utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we deal with a few housekeeping issues before we start. First of all, there is a point that I would like to raise with the parties relating to the agreed facts. In the agreed facts mentioned in the opening statement of Mr. Milan Martic on the 13th of December, there are a few things -- one thing that he mentioned that seemed to be the same as what is mentioned in the indictment and yet that fact has not been admitted. I just want to find out what the parties have to say about it. First of all, paragraph 67 of the amended indictment mentions both a referendum held in Croatia on the 19th of May, 1991, and declarations of independence by Croatia and Slovenia on the 25th of June, 1991. And in his opening statement, the accused clearly referred to declarations of independence by Croatia and Slovenia. Now, I refer here to transcript page 301, paragraph 1.7 to 11. It looks to me that a logical conclusion would be that both parties are not in dispute regarding Croatia and Slovenia's declaration of independence on the 25th of June, 1991. However, the list of agreed facts includes only the 19th of May, 1991 referendum in Croatia and does not refer to the 25th of June, 1991 declarations of independence where Croatia and Slovenia. Accordingly, it is the view of the Chamber that on this point the parties need to state whether they are agreed or not agreed on this fact. If you look at the agreed facts -- yeah. They said that on the agreed facts it is still that on the 19th of May, 1991 a referendum was held in Croatia except in dominantly Serb areas of the SAO Krajina, concerning independence of Croatia from Yugoslavia. And then the indictment says on the 19th of May, 1991, Croatia held a referendum in which the electorate voted overwhelmingly for independence from the SFRY, and on the 25th of June, 1991, Croatia and Slovenia declared their independence from Yugoslavia. The opening statement says in 1990 and in 1991 in the territories of the former Yugoslavia, there was an eruption of separatist movements in both Croatia and Slovenia. On that very same day, the 25th of June, 1991, Croatia and Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia. Is there any -- am I right to say that there seems to be some kind of agreement, although the formal answer was that there is no agreement on that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think Your Honour is correct. Obviously the Prosecution agrees with that fact and would be happy to agree -- agree it with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Your Honours, with respect to this issue, we have communicated, both in writing and directly, with the Office of the Prosecutor. There is no dispute about the fact that on that date, both Croatia and Slovenia declared independence. What is at issue legally is whether at the time that independence was declared Yugoslavia was a sovereign state or not with its constitution being applied on its entire territory. If this was the case, and in 1991 Yugoslavia was a member of the UN and the only internationally recognised state, it is very important to say that this declaration of independence was unconstitutional. The constitution of Yugoslavia did provide for the possibility of secession, but only according to the procedure prescribed by the constitution. The way this was done was unconstitutional, and these two republics had no right to do any such thing without the agreement of all the republics and a referendum held on the entire territory of Yugoslavia. The Defence wishes to say that there is no dispute, that as such a declaration was made on that day, but we wish to point out that this ran counter to international law and the constitution. This is the point at issue, and we feel that this is a very important issue, both factually and legally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. The next point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So for purposes of the proceedings, we then record that the parties are agreed that on that day Croatia and Slovenia did declare independence. As to the constitutionality thereof, I suppose it's a matter that will be dealt with in evidence and in argument. Thank you. The next point is a point of clarification. In the opening statement, the accused described the movement of the Serbs in Croatia to what's now cultural autonomy at an early stage as follows: "The Serbs in Croatia responded to this attitude of Croatian government by showing their support for preservation of Yugoslavia as a federal state with existing federal units. The Serbs demanded to have their own cultural autonomy within the Republic of Croatia. We are talking here about the cultural autonomy. In the case of disintegration of the Yugoslavia state, the Serbs in Krajina wanted the same principle to be applied as the principle used for self-determination of Croats and Slovenes. They wanted the same benefits to apply to them within Croatia. The Serbs in Krajina within their ethnic territory wanted protection for themselves, both territorial and institutional." On the other hand, the relevant part of paragraph 4 of the agreed facts lists -- I beg your pardon. Agreed facts list reads: "Finally the declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian people stated that if Yugoslavia remained to be a federation, the Serbs in Croatia would demand cultural autonomy, but if Yugoslavia became a federation, they had the right to political and territorial autonomy." Now, this last sentence doesn't make logical sense because they say: "If Yugoslavia remained a federation, the Serbs want cultural autonomy. Again, if it remained a federation, became a federation, they want territorial autonomy. There's no logical sense in that statement, and hence we ask for clarification. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Court is correct. There's I think a typographical error. I don't know what the word is there, but it's something different -- in the second part, it's something different than "federation," and we can -- I can get what it's supposed to say at the next break and we can have that for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I will take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next point --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, perhaps I could clarify. From our conversations, it transpires quite clearly that if a federation remained, the Serbs in Croatia wanted cultural autonomy. However, if there was a confederation, and this is evidently where the typographical error crept in, if a confederation was created, in that case the Serbs would demand territorial autonomy. However, if this is still a dispute, of course it's open to discussion. But this is our position as the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Milovancevic. I don't think the issue is one of dispute; it's just a question of clarification. It looks like your opposite number would like to investigate it further, and I hope that during the next break he will probably confer with you. And if you agree, both of you, that your interpretation or your explanation is a correct one, you'll confirm it at the next session. Is that correct so, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next issue relates to the examination of expert witnesses. In its decision on the 13th of January, the Trial Chamber considered that the focus of Rules 92 bis (E) and 94 bis is on the expert report and transcripts of previous testimony and not on supporting documents. The Trial Chamber would therefore like to clarify the procedure for examining expert witnesses in light of the fact that the first expert witness will be coming to testify very shortly. (1), once a witness is confirmed as an expert witness, the expert report is the core piece of documentary evidence for this witness. (2), the Prosecution is therefore requested to confine its examination-in-chief to the most relevant conclusions of the expert report, and in particular focus should be on matters which are likely to be controversial or which require further illustration and clarification by the expert. (3), as regards documents that the expert has used to prepare his or her report, the Prosecution is requested to limit its tendering of documents to those which are necessary for the illustrations of the matters referred to in point (2) above. And (4), following the ordinary procedure for cross-examination, the Defence may tender into evidence any documents, including those referred to in the expert report, which the Prosecution has not tendered into evidence. However, the Defence is also asked to confine its tendering of documents to matters of conclusion in paragraph (2) above. And finally, (5), the Trial Chamber will decide on the admissibility of documents which the Defence is subjected to after the testimony of the expert has been concluded. Are we happy with that arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I actually was prepared to -- and would still like to urge a different course on the Court, and that is what the Prosecution would like to do is to seek the admission of all the documents that the report relies upon into evidence. And I think that we have a good basis for it, and I think it would be an expedient use of the Court's time rather than a waste of the Court's time. And I know it appears as though the Court is going to be buried in documents, but in fact I think it will move things along more quickly. There are approximately 300 documents at issue. And the reason that the -- there are several reasons why the Prosecution would like to take this course, a course which has been adopted in other proceedings. The first is that the Defence -- and this is particularly -- I'm only speaking about the first expert who is going to testify, who crucially is an in-house expert. He is an employee of the Office of the Prosecution. The Defence has already challenged his impartiality. Now, I know that that challenge came in the context of whether the report would be admitted into evidence; the Court rejected that challenge. However, that challenge obviously still exists with respect to the weight that the Court should accord the report and the conclusions drawn by the Court. We think that it's going to be very important for the Court to have available to it the documentation that the expert relied upon in order to rebut this challenge from the Defence as to the impartiality or partiality of this expert. And it's hard to tell which -- right now which documents may become important to the Court's evaluation of the expert, which is why we think the Court should have available to it all of the documentation so it can check to see if the expert has drawn reasonable conclusions from the documentation. That's only the first point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the Court respond to that point that you've just made --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- before we go to the next one. What you have just said is precisely what the Court fears, that it be inundated with a whole voluminous bunch of documentation and the Prosecution says, Court, there are the documents. You make a peek, go through them and find out what is relevant and what is not relevant. I think the Prosecution must come to Court with its case well prepared and be able to say: For conclusion A of the expert, the facts supporting that are found in document C, that is an annex, not to say: There are documents C up to Z, and the Court must find which document is relevant for that conclusion. We -- the problem here is if you are going to be filing or tendering 300 documents and you do not -- the Prosecution itself does not even know which of the documents it relies on for the conclusions that the expert comes to and it expects the Court to wade through those documents, then obviously you are getting documents into evidence through the backdoor. I would rather that those documents on which the expert bases his conclusions on be referred to in his evidence in chief, those documents be marked, and those documents be looked at and be admitted into evidence. If you want other documents to be marked for identification, they can be marked for identification, and the admissibility may be argued later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't my intention for a moment to suggest that we were just going to dump the documents on the Court and let the Court find its way. I think, number one, the report is quite clear in terms of it's very extensively footnoted. It's clear which documents are relied upon for which conclusions. It's also our full intention in the examination-in-chief to focus the Court on the most important, most relevant documents. However, this is precisely the point. We would like in the examination-in-chief to be able to focus on the most relevant documents without having to try to get the full -- go through each document that the report relies on, spend days on end going through each document, supporting each document, how each document supports a particular conclusion, then move to admit that document into evidence until we finally get to 300 documents. We don't want to waste the Court's time that way or the parties' time. We would like to focus in on the discussion on the most important documents. The point I was trying to make is, number one, in the report itself, which -- and we're not going to touch on every conclusion in the report; it's an extensive report. There are footnotes citing documents. It may be that the Court will later on be looking at a particular issue, take an interest in it, want to see if the conclusion is supported by the document, and have that available to it. I'm not suggesting it go any further than that. The second point, Your Honour, is that there are a number of other witnesses who will testify about these documents. And we think that it is expedient to try to get the documents into evidence now and then allow the witnesses to be able to go back and comment on some or all of those documents. The point is the admissibility, the threshold for admissibility, is -- we think should be quite low. These documents have not been challenged. Their authenticity has not been challenged. They were put on our exhibit list. It was contemplated from the beginning that they would be exhibited. They were disclosed to the Defence. They have not been challenged in terms of their authenticity. They should be presumed authentic. They were important. They were relied upon for the report. They should come into evidence. As far as what weight they get or how they ultimately figure at the end, that is a separate matter, and that will depend on what the report says, that will depend on what witnesses say later, that will depend on the conclusions of the Court. And it is our intention to direct the Court, and I'm sure the Defence will do the same, to those matters as we go, both in terms of the examination of the expert but also in the final brief and final arguments. We will direct the Court to relevant documents. We are not going to dump the documents on the Court and hope that the Court finds its way. That's not our intention at all. It just seems to us that getting these documents in in one group, rather than spending time going over each one and having the expert testify about each one in his testimony is the most expedient way to proceed. Bring -- let them come into evidence in a group. He will testify about the most important ones. They will be available to the Court that way, and other witnesses can then testify about them later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the second point that you've raised, let me just ask a question: Why can't those documents that are going to be referred to by other witnesses be tendered into evidence through those witnesses rather than through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It could be done that way, Your Honour. I just think it's more -- I'm certainly not disputing that it could be done that way. I just am suggesting that it be more expedient to have these documents in evidence, available to all the parties to be able to argue about, available for witnesses to be able to comment on. We would get that kind of matter out of the way, and I suggest that we could get through the expert's testimony much more quickly if we do it that way then if we have to go through each document through his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that expedience must override procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I'm suggesting that expediency is a consideration in procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- would you like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is the view of the Defence that the standpoint of the Chamber in this issue is completely in accordance with what the practice should be before this Tribunal. The arguments of the Prosecutor, with all due respect, is something that we feel cannot be accepted. It's a completely separate issue, the issue of the value, content, weight of an expert report, an expert who has knowledge and expertise not otherwise available to the Chamber. It is his task to draw the Chamber's attention to the documents he used. This does not automatically mean that the expert should comment on each and every document; that would be pointless. But he should explain how he came to the conclusions he reached. This looks like an attempt to tender in advance something that should only be done during the cross-examination. The issue of the content of the expert report and its value and weight is a separate issue from the issue of admissibility of documents, the documents referred to by the expert. These are all separate issues. We feel that the Chamber's position is quite correct when it comes to dealing with expert reports. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The Chamber took the opportunity to raise this issue this early with the parties so that the parties can adjust their positions accordingly. We're not going to rule on it right now, if there's any need for ruling at all. The expert witness is not about to be called just now, so I would suggest that the parties think about it and maybe just before they call the first expert witness, state their position to the Court and maybe the Court might make a ruling at that stage, if there's any need for that. For the time being it's just for the parties just to consider. At this stage, in view of what has been reported to the Chamber about the witness who's about to be called, I would like the court to go into private session. Will the court please go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the pre-trial conference and then just before the opening statements in this case back in December, the Chamber raised a number of matters that it asked the parties to try to seek agreement on. And the Court indicated that it would check back with us -- I thought maybe I would take the initiative and report to the Court where we stand on those matters. I'm -- I regret to report that the progress has been exactly zero in reaching agreement in any of those matters. And I think it's not through any failure of trying by the Prosecution. We sent a letter to the Defence on the 2nd of January of this year asking if they would agree to any of the things that the Court raised, specifically -- and then we -- we have received a reply today to our request. Specifically we asked if the -- if the Defence would agree that in fact there was an armed conflict in Croatia during the relevant time, that is, from August of 1991 until August of 1995. The Defence has replied that they are unable to agree to that, which -- well, I'll leave comment aside, but that's what the -- what the response has been back from the Defence. The Court also asked us to see if we could agree with respect to victims in this case, on a list of victims. And from the point of view of the Prosecution, the easiest, most efficient way to do that would be for the parties simply to agree on the testimony of the experts which is about the victims and which identifies the victims from exhumations and so forth. And to that end the Prosecution asks the Defence if they would agree to the testimony of the experts, which of course they -- as the Court is well aware, they have previously specifically not agreed to their reports and their testimony. They continue to adhere to their position, have not agreed to the experts, and want to cross-examine all three of the experts. In the view of the Prosecution, under Rule 94 bis there's no avenue for the Prosecution to move for the admission of those reports and testimony without cross-examination. 94 bis doesn't seem to allow that, and the Court has ruled on this matter, so I don't see any way forward on this issue. The Court also asked if we would agree on what we call the intercept witnesses, MM16, 17, and 18. We asked the Defence if they would agree to the testimony of those intercept witnesses and the admission into evidence of the relevant intercepts, which of course we could argue about later, what they mean and so forth. The Defence has declined to agree to that. Again, I don't think there is an avenue under the Rules for the Prosecution to move for the admission of these witnesses. 92 bis is not really applicable here in our view, so we're going to have to call those witnesses. The Chamber also asked if the parties would agree -- consider Rule 92 bis for the following witnesses: 28, 64, and 74. The Prosecution's position, after consideration of this suggestion from the Trial Chamber, was that we would in fact agree to Rule 92 bis for witness 28. However -- and we asked the Defence if they would agree to that witness to be 92 bis. With respect to 64 and 74, it's the view of the Prosecution that those witnesses are critical and need to be heard live by the Chamber. However, those two witnesses are -- testify about the Zagreb shelling. The Prosecution identified three other witnesses, 68, 72, and 73, on the Zagreb shelling that we do believe could be admitted via 92 bis. We asked the Defence if they would agree to the admission via 92 bis of those witnesses. The Defence at this time declined to agree on any of those witnesses. Here we do have a way forward from the Prosecution's side, and we will file a motion shortly seeking the admission via Rule 92 bis of those four witnesses. That is 28, 68, 72, and 73. I expect we will file that motion within the next few days. Finally, Your Honours, we have prepared a book of maps that we think would be helpful to the Trial Chamber that we expect a number of witnesses to comment on and to speak about and testify about. This is something that has been done in a number of cases recently for the convenience of the parties. It's been thought helpful to have -- and for the Chamber to have a number of the critical maps contained in one binder, become one exhibit, that everybody can then have a copy of and refer to. And with the Court's permission I'd like to hand up our proposed map book for the Chamber to have a look at. If the usher -- we have it over here, if the usher could -- this, obviously, has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we hand it out, let's just hear what the Defence has to say on it being handed up. Mr. Milovancevic. Just on the map, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have received the proposal of the OTP on Friday, as a matter of fact. We looked at this very carefully. These are the documents that are supposed to be used in these proceedings before this highest of legal institutions. We spoke to the Prosecution about this, and if the Trial Chamber is interested, we can voice our objections now, each and every one of them, because they are totally arbitrary, these maps. You cannot make a survey, for example, of certain municipalities in Croatia with a majority Serb population on the basis of the vote in 1990. Please, Your Honours, isn't this an elementary thing that the ethnic make-up of municipalities is ascertained by way of a description, not voting? Of course it was not our intention to deny things per se, but we wanted the names of the maps to be adjusted to what is contained in the maps. We want this to be as precise as possible and to say that the map was from 1991, 1992, 1993, whatever year, with borders from such-and-such a period and so on and so forth. These are very specific objections, and I don't want to tire the Trial Chamber with all of these details, but if the Trial Chamber considers this necessary, I can deal with each and every map individually now. I don't know whether you have these maps in front of you now, but I can give you an example, for instance. We were offered a map of the Western Balkans. There is no such term. Please. And it is a map of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia actually and with its specified borders. So what's this all about? If some countries are on a map, then one should say: This is a map with the borders of Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia, and so on. But if what is denoted are the contours of the former Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as a member of the UN, then it should say, "the borders of Yugoslavia for 1991." But to say that this is a map of the Western Balkans, that doesn't mean a thing to us, and it leads us to possible inferences and conclusions that can be very delicate in such proceedings. We tried to deal with these issues very seriously. Perhaps it does not appear to be that serious, but it's a very, very delicate issue, and that is why the Defence presented its position on it very clearly, and we submitted that to the OTP. We also tried to help our colleagues from the OTP, how they should mark these maps so that we could accept them as such. I think that that is quite do-able, especially through a normal conversation. I don't think it's right to cast blame this way, but I hope that we get things going eventually. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We hear what you say, Mr. Milovancevic, about maybe solving the problem by way of a discussion with the Prosecution and trying to re-name the maps properly as being the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia instead of Western Balkans or whatever corrections need to be made. The Chamber will recommend that the parties meet and try to resolve that issue, the naming of the maps and making sure that they are absolutely correct before they are handed up to Court. And if the parties are not able to do that, the Court will have to rule on this issue at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, just a few words about what our colleagues from the Prosecution said about the other facts. There are facts on which it is possible to agree, and there are others on which it is impossible to agree. As for our disagreement with the definition of the armed conflict that was offered to us, we wrote what we had to write very precisely, trying to be very precise legally and factually. Secondly, as for the victims, the OTP believes that we should agree on the victims on the basis of the findings of their experts. We will be in a position to agree on such matters only once our medical experts complete their work, because we got material from the OTP stating that their reports on the victims, names, et cetera, all of the things that have to do with victims, casualties, there are many mistakes involved. So we don't have to act in haste. We need to double-check all of this with our own experts. Also, the witness statements. May I just note one point, Your Honour. I don't want you to get the wrong picture about what the Defence is doing. We were here on the 12th and 13th last time, and then we returned to Belgrade on the 14th of December. Since then there were many holidays, including the Christmas and new year holidays. The Defence tried to make up for time lost and to pack its office. I'm not referring to shelves and cupboards, but I'm referring to the written materials that have to do with this case. I have to indicate one particular thing, that these materials have been brought to The Hague. It's half a tonne of material, 230 binders. We don't have the technical facilities to set up an office here. Of course we know this is no concern of the Trial Chamber's, but we asked the registry to assist us. We don't want to burden the Trial Chamber with this, but this is an actual fact of life that the -- that should be taken into account because it makes our life difficult. Today we will be able to deal with one witness only, and all the rest of our material is stored. It's in storage, it's locked up. All our things that were brought from Serbia are in storage here. Just one more thing. This is the very beginning of these proceedings. Time and work will show what we can agree upon. Since our client is in detention, we have no reason to obstruct the proceedings or to drag our feet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Obviously at this stage of the trial, those points, those four points, that the Trial Chamber had asked that the parties try to reach agreement on have not been agreed upon, and the only way forward at this stage is that the Prosecution must proceed and prove its case as best it can. And if there's any agreement that the parties might reach as the proceedings go -- progress, so be it. Mr. Whiting, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We call our first witness, Your Honour. Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, can I be guided on when the Court intends to take its first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One and a half hours is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One and a half hours. Well, we've just gone beyond an hour -- no, we started at half past, we haven't an hour yet. So we will go for the remainder of the one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may ask the witness to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, in the last court the Judge asked the witness to do that, but I'm happy to do that. Witness, could you read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You may be seated. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If at any time you cannot understand me or you're not getting the translation, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: My name is Veljko Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The 19th of March, 1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you a Serb of Croatian nationality?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you currently live in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before the war, could you tell us what your professional was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I have a university degree in forestry, and I ran a forestry company in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did that -- where in Croatia did that company operate?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In Pakrac, Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what -- is that the job that you had in 1990/1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until what date did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I held that position until the 19th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before the war, were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when the Serbian Democratic Party, known as the SDS, was formed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In Croatia it was established sometime in February 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where was that? Where was it first formed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were the leaders of the SDS in Knin who first formed the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The president of the party of the Jovan Raskovic. Among them were Dusan Zelembaba, Jovan Opacic, Milan Babic, Djoko Vjestica, Macura, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when the first multi-party elections were held in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, they were held sometime in the spring of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall how the SDS performed in those elections?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, the SDS won in the municipalities of Benkovac, Knin, Gracac, and Lopac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you, yourself, joined the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. That was at the end of May 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, because we saw that the party that we, most of the Serbs, gave our vote to, the SDP, and those moments after the elections did not sufficiently follow the problems that the Serbs were facing. And we thought that it was important for the Serbs to get organised so they could present their interests in a better and easier manner, everything that was relevant to their lives, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You referred in your answer to the SDP. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Change. The League of Communists tried to democratise into a new party, and that's the name of the party to this day, the SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also referred to the problems that the Serbs were facing. Could you tell us what, in your view, those problems were?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, first of all these election rallies where the new iconography appeared that was reminiscent of the recent past of the Second World War. Then Croatian politicians spoke of the over-representation of Serbs in the police and different companies, et cetera. There were quite a few negative connotations in these speeches. Also, the constitution was changed, and this party did not express an interest in the Serbs who built their past together with the Croats, and we realised that they did not sufficiently monitor the problems facing the Serb community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, I would like to go through with you the different positions that you held in the party, in the SDS, and also later in politics. And then -- and also some of the things that happened to you as a result of your positions and then go back over the history again in a little more detail. When you joined the SDS, did you hold a position in the party?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: First I was a member of the Regional Board of the SDS for Western Slavonia, later on the president of the Regional Board, and then I became a member of the Executive Board of the party for the whole of Croatia, due to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the Regional Board of the SDS? When did you first become a member?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I became a member of the Regional Board as soon as June 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did you become president of the Regional Board?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did you become a member of the Executive Board for the whole of Croatia? Was that also at the same time? At the end of 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, initially when the SDS was founded in the area of Western Slavonia, did the SDS in that area cover only Western Slavonia or a larger area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: At that time, the party was for the whole of Slavonia and Baranja, stretching from Ilok to Kutina, encompassing 14 or 15 municipalities and cities. Later on there was a division into Western Slavonia and Eastern Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that occur, just the date?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: That occurred in 1991. I think it was in May when the national council of eastern -- or rather, of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was declared. After that, we promulgated Western Slavonia so that we would not be under the competence of that body and Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment. Do you recall at the end of 1990 the so-called SAO Krajina being formed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was the president of the SAO Krajina when it was first formed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it was not until 1991 that the SAO Western Slavonia was formed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 12th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And before that occurred, was the SAO for Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem formed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it was formed in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was the president of that SAO?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the SAO Western Slavonia was formed in August of 1991, who was the president of that entity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, what municipalities were included within the SAO Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Pakrac, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Podravska Slatina, parts of Orahovica, and Okucani. Until then it had not been a municipality, but it comprised the villages between Nova Gradiska and Novska, and then Okucani was considered a municipality, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned Pakrac. Was -- before the SAO Western Slavonia was formed, was Pakrac in another SAO?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Pakrac municipality on the 18th or 21st of February, 1991, acceded to the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when the SAO Western Slavonia was formed, it shifted from the SAO Krajina over to the SAO Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court in general terms, just briefly, and obviously we'll have more detail about this later, your -- describe for the Court your political approach that you advocated in 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: My political approach, first of all, was that all the issues that had emerged had to be resolved through dialogue. That's why there was a clash with Milan Babic within the party. The members of the Regional Board of the SDS of Western Slavonia maintained contacts with the representatives of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, and this was held against us by the SDS in Knin. The member of the Regional Board, Professor Vojo Vukicevic, who went to negotiate in Zagreb, was criticised for this and had to leave both the party and Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are there other leaders or persons within the SDS and Western Slavonia who you can identify that took your approach?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a few of them. Dusan Ecimovic, Obrad Ivanovic, Veljko Vukic, Milenko Miletic, people from Kutina, Branko Popovic from Grubisno Polje. Zivko Zagorac from Grubisno Polje. I would say they were in the majority, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You made reference to other leaders, and you specified Milan Babic, who took a different approach. How would you describe this different approach?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They had no wish or desire to negotiate with Zagreb about the various opinions and approaches that had emerged. They wanted to break off all contact with Zagreb and to resolve everything within our own community. For example, there was an event when Serbs from Vukovar came to a meeting in Knin, and the Serbs in the Knin SDS said they were Ustasha because the checker-board flag was flown in Vukovar. And the difference -- there was a difference that emerged between us and Babic's people from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were -- you've mentioned Babic. Who were some of the other leaders who espoused this different approach?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Bosko Bozanic from Korenica, David Rastovic from Lapac, Djoko Vjestica. I can't recall all the names at present. But people from Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, Lapac, Korenica, the areas of Dalmatia and Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How about Milan Martic. Which approach did he take? Did he tend to take our approach or the approach that you've just described that was taken by leaders in Knin?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: When Milan Martic emerged on the political scene, he was in favour of the same option as Milan Babic, not to negotiate with Zagreb, but to resolve all issues within the Krajina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In July of 1991, did you form something called the Serbian Democratic Forum?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. It was established in early July 1991 in Lipik, which was then part of Pakrac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, what the purpose of the Serbian Democratic Forum was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: There was a division within the SDS in Croatia into the SDS of Krajina and the rest of the SDS in the Republic of Croatia. We wanted to strengthen the latter with independent intellectuals from the Republic of Croatia who wanted us to be united about Serbian interests all over Croatia, to articulate them together, to seek solutions through democratic dialogue. One could see that war was in the offing, and we received significant support from the Serbian intellectual elite in Zagreb and other cities. This was the occasion for the meeting. We tried to have a joint platform for dialogue with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I understand your answer, but I want to press just a little bit. You said that you -- that one could see that war was in the offing. Was this initiative, the Serbian Democratic Forum, an attempt to avert war or was it an attempt to promote war? What was it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Certainly the initiative was to prevent war, and by putting forward our positions and ideas, to let the general public in Croatia, both Serbs and Croats, know that there had to be a peaceful solution and that we had to search for a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was your role in the founding of the Serbian Democratic Forum?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was in the steering committee. I was one of the organisers. We couldn't hold a meeting in Banija and Kordun as planned, so we held it in Western Slavonia. I provided all the logistical support, and I went to negotiations both in Zagreb and Belgrade with other members of the board in order to prepare for the founding meeting of the Serb Democratic Forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzakula, you said you couldn't hold the meeting in Banija and Kordun as planned. Why not?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: A letter arrived. My friends in Zagreb received it from the SDS of Krajina, banning the holding of such a meeting on the territory of the SAO Krajina. It had to be held somewhere else in the Republic of Croatia. Their policy, and as they then said the people of the SAO Krajina did not want this "democratic" meeting to be held in Krajina because they no longer wanted any contacts with fascist Croatia, and if we wished to do so, we should do it elsewhere, not on the territory of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, did you provide this letter that you've referred to to the Office of the Prosecution two days ago in your witness preparation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could -- this document has already been provided to the Defence, and I would like to hand up copies and provide a copy to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the record, the document has been ERNed 04666700. Of course, since we received it only on Saturday, it has not been put into the E-court system, so we don't have an opportunity to test-drive that system quite yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it being handed in as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to tender it as an exhibit once the witness has identified it and looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, is this the letter that you provided to the Office of the Prosecution on Saturday, this last Saturday?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that it was a letter from the Serbian Democratic Party of Krajina, prohibiting the Serbian Democratic Forum from meeting and holding an initiating meeting within the Krajina. The letter is signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The letter was signed by Dr. Ljubica Solaja, president of the SDS of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what relationship did that person have with Milan Babic, if any?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: She was a close associate. She couldn't have been president of the Krajina SDS if she had not been appointed by Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just, for the benefit of the Court, read the next-to-last paragraph which starts: "The attributes of that forum," referring to the Serbian Democratic Forum.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The attributes of the forum, Serbian and democratic, do not correspond to its actual role. It is not democratic because it is aimed at rendering null and void the democratically expressed will of the Serbian people not to live in the independent state of Croatia. In our evaluation, for this reason, it is destructively totalitarian and defeatist. It is not Serbian because it is working against the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you receive this letter, Mr. Dzakula?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Is received this letter later on from the first president of the Serbian Democratic Forum. They told me they had received the letter and the prohibition towards the end of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this letter into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any comments, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The letter is then admitted into evidence and given exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit Number 1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit Number 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, who were the other participants in the Serbian Democratic Forum?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Among the founders were Professor Svetozar Livada, Milivoj Pupovac, Nikica Vujnovic, Obrad Ivanovic, Nadezda Gace, Mladen Mirevkovic [phoen], the late Vladimir Ivkovic, Dusan Zelembaba, and Professor Jovan Raskovic was the president of the SDS for all of Croatia. Then there was Dusan Starcevic and Jovo Opacic. And it was very important that we had the president and the leaders of the SDS in Croatia as well as independent intellectuals, and we also had the support of Professor Gajo Petrovic and other influential Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you try to get support for this initiative either from Croatia -- from the Government of Croatia or from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This group, which was the steering committee, went both to Zagreb, the parliament, and the government of the Republic of Croatia, where we spoke to Mr. Lerotic, President Tudjman's advisors, and we also went to Belgrade where we had talks with Budimir Kosutic, who was the deputy prime minister of the Republika Srpska. They both listened to what we said, but neither side gave us any significant support. And when we issued our communique, there was a media blockade both in Belgrade and in Zagreb. So we did not get the kind of support we expected and hoped for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of President Tudjman's advisors. Just for the record, I want to be clear on what that name is. If you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Lerotic. I cannot remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Sir, do you know a person by the name of Jovo Vezmar?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1991, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He was the chief of police, the most important person in the police in Pakrac municipality. I'm not sure of his exact title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you had an encounter with him with regard to the Serbian Democratic Forum?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. This was in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I received an invitation from his late brother to go to the village of Kraguj, to the village community hall, for a conversation with the citizens there. However, when I arrived there was only Jovo Vezmar there, and he had been absent from the area for several months. We greeted one another briefly, and then he told me -- he said the following: It's your fault and you're responsible for the fact that these five municipalities have become passive and that war has not broken out in them. You have 24 hours to resign from your job in the company, to resign from your political positions, and to leave Pakrac municipality, otherwise you will be killed. I asked him twice whether he knew what he was talking about, and he said he did and he said that that was what I must do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I obeyed him, yes. On the following morning, I called up my managing director in Bjelovar. I asked him for annual leave; he approved it. And in the afternoon I left Pakrac. But I did not resign from my political positions and I did not give up my job; I only took annual leave. So I only partially obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I went to Beograd to report to the president of the SDS, Professor Jovan Raskovic. I told him about this problem, and he told me to hide somewhere in Serbia, to go to a village, until he re-called me to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell me again where you went, what city?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I went to Vrnjacka Banja in the south of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, but first where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: To Belgrade. To Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. How long -- did you eventually return to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, some 10 or 15 days later I returned to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened when you returned?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: When I returned, I saw my friends in the SDS. We analysed the situation. War had already broken out, both in Eastern Slavonia and in Krajina. We held a session for Western Slavonia, a session for the Regional Broad, and we promulgated the SAO of Western Slavonia, this was in August, on the 12th of August, in order to organise and to begin negotiations with the Government of Croatia in order to prevent war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you became at that time president of the SAO Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have a further conversation with Jovo Vezmar?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Later on I met him again, on the 18th of August, in the evening. I was brought in by two of his fellow fighters. They were armed. They took me to his headquarters, and he told me that in the morning they were setting out to war and that I had to decide whether I was with them or not. And if I tried anything, I would be killed. I was detained until the afternoon of the following day, when the first attack on Pakrac was already over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Court stands adjourned, 20 minutes -- it's a 20-minute adjournment, is it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is reminded that he's still bound by the declaration that he made at the beginning of his testimony. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I proceed, if I could just update the Court. The Prosecution and the Defence did have a brief discussion about that matter that was raised, the agreed fact, and the need for a clarification. A further discussion is required. I think we'll have an answer by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, before we -- before the recess, you had told us about the founding of the Serbian Democratic Forum and the reaction -- some of the reactions to that in 1991. Does the Serbian Democratic Forum still exist today?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it still exists. This year we are celebrating our 15th anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have a position in the Serbian Democratic Forum?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm president of the Executive Board of the Serb Democratic Forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what it does today. What is its function today?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The SDF is first and foremost a non-governmental/non-profit organisation. It deals with refugee flows and gives legal aid free of charge. We are engaged in humanitarian activity. We have social welfare programmes for the old and weak, and also we have development programmes helping people to find jobs for themselves and resolve important questions to their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What relationship does the SDF have with the Croatian government, both at the republic level and at the local level?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: For the past few years we have cooperated well with the various ministries of the government of the Republic of Croatia, first of all, the ministry of reconstruction, then the ministry of welfare and health care, and also at the local level, at county and municipal level, and we also cooperate with international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Like which ones?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I spoke too quickly. Like which international organisations?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: First of all, the UNHCR, US Aid, OSCE, the European Commission, through its various projects, and most European embassies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many offices does SDF have in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: We have 18 offices in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it one of the biggest NGOs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, the biggest and the oldest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1991. At the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or the RSK, was formed. Did you have a position in that entity?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, when the RSK was formed, this was on the 26th of February, I believe, 1992. I, on behalf of Western Slavonia, became part of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which also included Eastern Slavonia and Krajina. It was one body, and it was the republican government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was your position when you became part of the government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was deputy prime minister in charge of agriculture, and specifically forestry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As deputy prime minister, did you attend sessions of the government of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I attended most sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were those held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Most often they were held in Knin. One, I think, or two perhaps were held in Eastern Slavonia and one was in Western Slavonia sometime towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll come back to that session that was held in Western Slavonia in 1992. Jumping ahead for a moment, did -- in February of 1993, were you -- did you still hold the position of deputy prime minister in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In February I was still deputy prime minister of the RSK, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1993. February 1993.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I'm the one who's sorry. 1993. Say until March 1993, so in February 1993 I still held the position of deputy prime minister of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that month, February 1993, did you sign something called the Daruvar Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 18th of February, 1993. It was signed in Doljani and it was called that Daruvar Agreement because it was in the municipality of Daruvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, what that agreement was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It was an agreement between the Serb and Croat sides, in which we agreed that by peaceful means and dialogue we would resolve all existing problems, utilities problems, water, electricity, roads, contacts between families at checkpoints. So I think it was on expression of good will, if I can put it that way, to open an dialogue between the Serb and the Croat sides. It was the first agreement of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who negotiated this agreement on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Dusan Ecimovic, Mladen Kunic. I can't remember now. There were two other people. My mind seems to have stopped now. There was a total of five people. I am sorry, but really, my mind has stopped. I can't remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you later if you -- if they've come back to your memory. And if you remember them, just please tell us. Were -- on the Croat side, who negotiated the agreement, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, on the Croat side there was Ivan Milas, as the representative of the government; then with him Josko Moric, assistant minister, and the mayors of Novska, Pakrac, Daruvar, Grubisno Polje, Slatina, and at this point I cannot remember their names because they were not that well-known to the political public at the time. I think that the last name of one of them was Kos; I seem to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were the negotiations for this agreement secret or public?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The preparations for this signing of the agreement were secret, but the agreement itself, as it was to be signed, was public. The president of the Assembly of Western Slavonia and the members of the Regional Board of Slavonia knew about it, and also we went in the middle of the day, we went out to sign it. People knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why were the preparations done in secret?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, we were in a delicate situation then. There was a war going on in Knin around Maslenica. Immediately after that, a few days later, the president of the republic, Goran Hadzic, gave instructions to the commander of the Krajina army, General Novakovic, that we in Western Slavonia should attack Novska and Nova Gradiska. A few times during the course of two or three days, these orders were issued and we as local leaderships opposed that kind of attack, explaining that there was no reason for that. We had to submit this in writing, that we guarantee peace and that there will not be a conflict. At that moment, in order to prevent a possible new outbreak of war, Mr. Gerald Fisher, the head of the sector and the commander of the army in that sector, General Zabala [phoen] proposed to me and to my associates that we should make another step in order to assure our own environment, referring to the Croat side, too, that we should start dialogue and that we should start specific agreements on the normalisation of relations. We thought about this for a long time and -- well, for a long time, one day, but in those circumstances it's a long time. We realised that we ran a risk but we realised that we had to accept that for the safety of our citizens and their lives so there would not be a new war, and this would not guarantee peace to anyone or even life as such. I and my associates supported that and went ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If other leaders in the RSK had known about this initiative, the Daruvar initiative, would they have supported it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They would not have supported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you give us an answer, which leaders are you speaking of? Which leaders would not have supported it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, Goran Hadzic, the then-president of the republic, then Zdravko Zekic, the prime minister, also the minister of defence, Spanovic, and the minister of police, Mr. Martic, knowing that General Novakovic was giving us orders, instructions, orders to attack, to wage war. And if they knew of this order and they probably supported it, I doubt that they would have supported our starting of negotiations at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the Daruvar agreement became public or was publicly signed, did something happen to you with respect to your position in the government?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: First of all, there was major consternation among the authorities of the Republic of the Serb Krajina, and a few days after that I was suspended from this position of deputy prime minister. And Mr. Dusan Ecimovic, who was minister in the government, was also suspended. Although it was illegal at the time, only the Assembly could have dismissed us, but they acted very quickly in order to prevent the implementation of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who suspended you, specifically?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, at that time I had two pieces of information, and they are still valid. Goran Hadzic and Mr. Zecevic. And also I was suspended from the position of the president of the regional council, and Dusan Ecimovic as a member and Mladen Kulic as president of the regional committee for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you said you were also suspended from the position of the president of the regional council. That's the regional council of the SDS, I take it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No. It was the regional council of the Serb region of Western Slavonia. There was Eastern Slavonia and Western Slavonia, and this was a small regional body in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you were dismissed from these positions, did you in 1993 hold any other political position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: After that, the Assembly passed a decision that elections could be held in Pakrac and Okucani, those two municipalities. And we availed ourselves of that legal possibility. We carried out elections, and in May 1993, by secret ballot, I was elected president of the Municipal Assembly of Pakrac. And I was president until the autumn of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen to you in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st of September, 1993, in the morning hours I was arrested by the assistant minister of Serb Krajina, Krsta Zarkovic, who brought a group of members of a special unit in Knin. They arrested me and took me to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described Krsta Zarkovic as an assistant minister. Assistant minister of what?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He was assistant minister of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he was an assistant to whom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He was assistant to the then-minister, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was arrested in a private house where I lived then in Japaga in Pakrac in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why a unit from Knin came to Western Slavonia to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, they came because they did not trust the local police to do that, because at that time I had quite a bit of authority in that area. So they brought units from elsewhere that were very well-armed, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said you were taken to Knin -- well, first of all, do you know why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, they didn't tell me a thing then. However, they treated me very harshly. They handcuffed me and took me to Knin. There I was told that I was a spy, that I was breaking up the republic, the state, and I was given a decision that an investigation would start against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who signed that decision, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The first paper, the decision, was signed by Aco Draca, who was a high official in the ministry of police. He was the head of the DB, that's what people said. I can't say exactly now whether he was assistant minister or something, but I know that he was the number one man in state security and he's the person who signed the order for arrest and for carrying out a police investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know the relationship at that time between Aco Draca and Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I was not aware of their personal relationship. I can only say that in such a situation a person who did not have the support of the minister, Mr. Milan Martic, could hardly have been in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Martic was aware of or involved in your arrest at this time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He certainly knew of it. And there would not have been an arrest without his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On what basis do you say that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, because none of them would have dared do that because they were aware of my role and position in my region, among my people, and it had to be someone who was in a high position in government. And President Zecevic also, and personally I was on good terms with him, he said that he could not have done anything about it, although he was against it, because it was only up to the minister of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said in your -- one of your earlier answers that you were accused of breaking up the republic. First of all, to be clear, which republic are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The Republic of Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was it ever specified in the communications to you during your arrest or in -- during interrogations why it was thought that you were trying to break up the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, the inspectors who were interrogating me thought that this document was a crime and that this signed agreement worked in favour of breaking up. They did not read it properly. They did not quote it properly, but they thought that the agreement itself was a crime, speaking of secession. Those were insinuations because there were no words to that effect in the agreement, but that is what they were saying to me and that is what I was suspected of having done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you talk about the agreement in your last answer, you're talking about the Daruvar Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I mean the Daruvar Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you were taken to Knin. What happened in Knin?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, in Knin I was in solitary confinement for four days while the police investigation was going on. I was brought to the inspectors who threatened me with automatic rifles, that it would be better for me to say what -- all the things that they already knew, because otherwise it would be very difficult. After four days I, was taken to Glina to the district prison there, and the court initiated an investigation then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know specifically where you were held in Knin?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In Knin I was kept in the basement cellar of the police station in town itself, in solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you held in Glina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They kept me in Glina to the 3rd of December, 1993, with a break of a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What -- tell us what happened during that break. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, during the investigation I and Mr. Mladen Kulic invoked our immunity as MPs because we were members of the Assembly of the RSK. Therefore, they did not have the right to arrest us and detain us for as long as we had this immunity, and the investigating judge rendered a decision that we should be set free. This was on the 2nd of October, 1993. We went home and changed vehicles, just in case, with our colleagues. Our colleagues who came to visit us were arrested, and as we were crossing the border between the RSK and Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were arrested again in Kostajnica and returned to the police station in Kostajnica, to a solitary cell, that is. After being kept there for a few hours, two policemen in camouflage uniforms came to get us. They handcuffed me and Mladen Kulic, and they drove us to Glina. As we were driving through Petrinja they took us to a forest where they first beat us up physically, stomped on us with their feet, and then they took us to Glina and handed us over to the prison there. So the court has released us, and the police again intercepted us, beat us up, and returned us to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The two policemen in camouflage uniforms, do you know anything about them, about what unit they were in or who they were subordinate to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I could not find out who they were, but in Glina when I described them, they told me that they belonged to Silt's group, that's what people were saying, and in Banija, in that area, he was a military-active person. I don't know whether that was his last name or his nickname, but I just heard of this person called Silt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was that group within the police, within the military, what -- where did they fit in, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The ministry of police. These were special units of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know to whom they were subordinated to, if they were special units of the police?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, all police units, including that one, were under the minister of police, Mr. Milan Martic, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you were taken back to Glina, were you taken back to the same jail you had been in before?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Kulic and I were taken to solitary confinement for a few days and then we were sent back to our cells again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And those cells were in the same jail that you had been in before?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did -- on Saturday, during your witness preparation, did you provide us with a second document, and this one relating to this -- this episode?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document has also obviously been provided to the Defence, and with the assistance of the usher I would like to hand it up to the Court and a copy to the witness, please. The ERN of this document is 04666768 to 6769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is an ERN?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- I'm at a loss to remember -- we use the acronym so much, I can't remember what it stands for. Somebody will help me on this. Evidence something number -- evidence registration number. Each document that comes into the building gets an ERN and it is a unique number so that it can be -- this is the only document in the building that has that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
