utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that document have a date on it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it does, the 18th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This is a decision extending custody of the kind we received while in prison in Glina. It lasted for 15 days while an investigation was ongoing. This is one of the documents I managed to preserve, and it speaks of the extension of custody pending investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to the second page of the document, and in the English translation it's also on the second page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may interrupt, shouldn't it be authenticated first and tendered before you're leading on the contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine. I certainly can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you obtain this document?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I received this document in court, either on the 18th of October or a day or two before that, and I was told that my detention had been extended until the 18th of November of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is the document from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It was issued by the district court in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And specifically by the Presiding Judge Avdaj Popov?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He was the president of the Chamber that issued this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document will be admitted into evidence as Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, could I draw your attention to the second page of the document, and the fourth paragraph. And on the English translation it's the second page, fifth paragraph. And I believe it starts: "According to the Criminal Code." If you could just read that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: "According to the criminal law, the perpetrators of the crime of threatening the territorial integrity, as in Article 116, paragraph 1, in connection with Article 139, paragraphs 3 and 2 of the Criminal Code, the death penalty may be handed down. As a state of war was declared on the 22nd of January, 1993, which is still ongoing, this is the legal qualification of the crime from Article 139, paragraphs 3 and 2 in connection with Article 116, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that document aside. Now, I believe you testified earlier that you were ultimately released on the 3rd of December, 1993. What happened after you were released?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: On the 3rd of December, when we were released, I was on my way home when I was brought in. This was in Donji Caglic in the Pakrac municipality in Western Slavonia. I was detained for two or three hours and interviewed, and then I was again released and allowed to go home. On the following day, my friends informed me, Ecimovic and Kulic who were in Okucani, that the minister of police, Milan Martic, had issued a warrant for another arrest against us. The two of them managed to escape to Serbia. I did not manage to leave Western Slavonia, and when my friends informed me a little too late, I managed to hide. And for about 50 days I was in hiding in Western Slavonia in a private shelter to avoid being re-arrested and detained again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After those 50 days, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Then I came out of hiding and my friends returned from Belgrade, and they told me that we should go together to Belgrade and speak on Studio B, to tell our fellow citizens what was happening. I didn't like this. I said it was too early to speak about this in public, but however at their insistence, I accompanied them to Belgrade. And on the 3rd of February, 1994, I spoke on the independent television station Studio B. This was a late-night show. It went on for about an hour or about an hour and a half, and I spoke about what was happening in the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I ask you what -- more specifically what you spoke about, could you tell the Court a little bit more about what Studio B is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Studio B I think was the only independent television station in Belgrade at the time. You couldn't receive it all over Serbia because its range was limited, but it gave independent news about events, both inside Serbia and elsewhere, for example, in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was not state controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So when you say "independent," you mean independent of the state?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you -- you said that you spoke about what was happening in the RSK. Could you be a little more specific about what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: We talked about the war; the exodus of the Serbs from Western Slavonia; about the Territorial Defence commanders waging the wars; about the Daruvar Agreement, which was the main topic; what it was; what it was about; and the sanctions we experienced, that is our arrest and detention. I remember I said Krajina could be saved by wisdom, not by weapons, that we should engage in dialogue rather than warfare, and that was the topic of our talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you talk about Milan Martic or Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Milan Babic and Milan Martic, inter alia, on that television show. I said that they were exclusive, intolerant, that they were not in favour of dialogue and negotiations, that they arrested us, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean by "exclusive"? That's the translation we got, is "exclusive."

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They liked to listen to themselves. They thought the truth was only what they thought was true. They did not want to negotiate with Croatia. They wanted there to be a state border, and that this was a fait accompli. They thought that anyone who engaged in negotiations with Croatia was a traitor and a spy and they used various other names to refer to such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You used the word "intolerant" in reference to Milan Babic and Milan Martic. You said that you used that word "intolerant." What did you mean by "intolerant"? How were they intolerant?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They were impulsive, they were quarrelsome. If they didn't like the opinion of someone else that was contrary to their own, they would enter into a conflict with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did something happen the next day after you spoke on Studio B?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The next day with Dusan Ecimovic, my friend, I was walking through Belgrade. We were discussing the television broadcast. And near the Yugoslav drama theatre in the centre of Belgrade, we were approached by four large men in civilian clothes. They grabbed me by the arm and they said they had a car parked there and that I should go with them. They did not show me any identification, they did not say who they were, and I refused to enter the car with them. A fight broke out between them and me, which went on for about 10 or 15 minutes. They beat me. They tore parts of my clothes off, and then they used the spray and they hit me very hard. We all fell down to the ground. They put handcuffs on my hands. They put my shirt and my sweater over my head. They shoved me into the car, and this was in broad daylight. They took me to a parking lot. I couldn't see exactly where because they put my clothes over my head. And in that parking lot, they beat me with pistol butts. After that, they put me into another car, and there were civilians there as well, but from their conversation I gathered that they were policemen from Eastern Slavonia and that they belonged to the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to the ministry. Along the way they beat me and said: You want to negotiate with Ustasha while we are at war with them. Our brothers are being killed and you want to negotiate. And they took me back to Knin via Bosnia and put me in prison in the basement of the police station. I spent a further four days there. I was alone there, and in the night I heard them beating people in other rooms. I didn't know who these people were, but I could hear the moans and the sounds of beating. The next day, in the morning or at around 1.00, two men in camouflage uniforms came and they took me out the back entrance, put me in a Lada Niva, drove me through a wood into a built-up area, where they left me in the car with an automatic rifle and a bottle of red wine. They went into the house that was nearby and came back about half an hour later. Maybe they thought I would get hold of the rifle. Later on I learned that they had taken me to the village of Nebljuse in Lika on the border with Bosnia near Bihac. Along the way they insulted me, hit me, and when we arrived in Nebljuse, they took me to a house and they spoke to me until the morning, saying that I was a traitor, a spy, that I had to be dealt with, and then they held me in that house in a private prison for about ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you forced to make a statement when you were being held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: On the day before the last day, I had bruises on my face. They came to put some make-up on my face and they gave me a list of questions and answers, the answers I was supposed to read out. And they were going to film this and use it as evidence against me. As I saw where I was, and this man Tesla, who was interrogating me for the second time, said only God and I know where you are and where you'll end up. So I read what they had written down because I felt this was the easiest course for me to take. I'd had enough of maltreatment. The next day they took me back to Glina into the district prison by car, and I spent a further ten days or so there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness map 01131342. This is in E-court, but I've been told that with maps it's better to do them on hard copy rather than E-court because it shows up too small in E-court. So if the witness could be provided with a copy of the map and put on the ELMO, and if the Court could be given the map as well. I don't know if Defence counsel need a copy of the map also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Make them an offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed that, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Make them an offer of a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, if Defence counsel could be provided a copy, that would be convenient. And I need a copy, too. Now, to see the map on the -- to see the markings that the witness makes on the ELMO, if -- if you switch to computer evidence on the monitor, then you'll be able to see what the witness does on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, have you seen this map before?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What does this map show? Specifically what is in -- what is shown in orange on this map?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The colour orange marks the territory under the control of the Serbian authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you take a marker and please mark an "A" on the area that was first known as the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: SAO Krajina was around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not seeing it. I'm sorry. I mislead you on this one. It's video evidence, not computer evidence. Computer evidence is E-court, when you see the document in E-court. But to see what he's marking on the ELMO, it's video evidence. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can he please start with his markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you -- could you show where you have marked "A" for SAO Krajina, please.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you mark a "B" on the SAO Western Slavonia, please.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And a "C" on the SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just interrupt your leading. It might perhaps be helpful if he could also draw the boundaries of "A," the boundaries of "B," and the boundaries of "C," just to see what area "A" represents, what area "B" represents, and what area "C" represents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, could you do that? Are you able to draw the boundaries of "A," "B," and "C"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As he understands them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start with "C." This border here --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Dzakula. First of all, the usher will need to move the -- we can't see it on the monitor, so if you could move the "C" to the middle. Thank you. And if you could, Mr. Dzakula, take the pen so we have a record of this and draw around the line there that is "C," the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as you knew it.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The border coincides with this present border here. If need be, I can draw along it. That is more or less the border of the SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. May I just interrupt. It doesn't show an area, it just shows one boundary. I would like to see the perimeter of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, if you could just finish drawing the boundary and draw the whole perimeter, please.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you could do the same for the SAO Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The SAO Western Slavonia was more or less this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just to hold you for a moment there and we'll finish this exercise. Now, there's -- within the area that you've just drawn, there's an area that's in orange and then there's an area that has lines on it. Are you aware of any difference or any significance to those two different areas?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The difference in colour means the following: What is in orange was under the control of the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The remaining part, which has lines on it, was an area that was under the control of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, because in military terms it had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did that occur? When did that part fall to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This happened in stages. First on the 15th of October, the area around Grubisno Polje. Then on the 15th of November, Daruvar. And later on, by the 15th of December, the area around Podravska Slatina and Pozega. The area in orange is what remained after the 24th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So all those dates that you gave just now, 15th of October and 15th of November, 15th of December, those are all in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. They all refer to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the area that's in orange within the "B" area within Western Slavonia, until when did that remain under the control of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It remained under the control of the RSK until the 24th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could just complete the exercise and draw a boundary around the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: These are the borders of the SAO Krajina in August and September, 1991, because the border changed. First it was this and then it spread. So now I'm drawing the final border, the SAO Krajina as far as I am able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if I might interrupt, Mr. Whiting, I'm sorry to do this to you. I think we are going to need to have all of this on E-court system so that the witness's markings can be inserted and be part of the record. This is just a document that he's doing there and it's not going to appear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I was going to move this document into evidence, and then I think what can happen is it can then be put into E-court, the document that's been marked. It doesn't need to be re-marked on to E-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I certainly will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I know this version of this map is quite small and is very hard to read, but could you take maybe a thinner -- I don't know if you have available a thinner pen. Are you able to find -- I just want to mark a few of the cities or towns or villages that you've been speaking about. Can you find Knin, first of all, on this map?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you put a number 1 next to that circle that you've drawn?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to find Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Coiled you draw a number 2 next to Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to find Glina.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you draw a 3 next to that.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this one might be more difficult, Nebljuse, are you able to find where it is or approximately where it is?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It's about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA

I'm now finished with the map with the witness and I'm prepared to tender it into evidence, unless the Court has further questions about locations or information on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court doesn't have any questions at this stage on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then I would move it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the map will be admitted into evidence as Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It can be taken off the ELMO. Thank you. Now, as I understand it, just to be clear about the procedures, this will now -- the document that he has marked, the version that he has marked, will now be scanned into evidence and will be available as an exhibit in evidence, so will be available to the Court and to the parties and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please remember to mark it Exhibit 3, the scanned copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's already been marked Exhibit 3, and that procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, in -- moving ahead now to May of 1995, you made reference to a date in May of 1995 when the SAO Western Slavonia fell to Croatian forces. That was a result of what operation on the part of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: First of all, a small correction. It was not the SAO Western Slavonia. It was a region. And the action started on the 1st of May, 2005 -- sorry, 1 -- in 1995, rather. It was preceded by blocking -- closing the highway, then there was shelling. The Pakrac district where I was remained surrounded for another three days, and then the last attack was carried out on the 4th of August -- sorry, oh my goodness. The 4th of May and -- 1995, and then that was in the hands of the Croatian army and police, Okucani, already on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that operation in May of 1995, do you know what it was called, what its name was?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. It is Operation Flash, very well-known, and it lasted four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you quite properly corrected me in the way I had phrased the question, you said that it was not the SAO Western Slavonia but it was a region. Is it fair to say that it was -- the region that was once known as the SAO Western Slavonia but was in 1995 part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I think you're putting words into the mouth of the witness. Why don't you just ask him what -- region of what was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought I was trying to -- I was just trying to clarify his answer. But could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let him clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you clarify, Mr. Dzakula, why it is -- why you said it is a region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of what was it a region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the region of Western Slavonia within the Republic of Serb Krajina. The region of Western Slavonia was taken over from the former SAO Western Slavonia when the three SAO united in a state which was called the Serb Krajina. Then "autonomous" was dropped from the name. It wasn't the Serb autonomous region, but the Serb region within the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as a part of Operation Flash did something happen to you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I shared the fate of another 1500 men who were arrested after that action and taken to different prisons. There were several prisons involved because not everybody could fit into one. I was taken to the police station in Pakrac, and the next day I was taken to Bjelovar for interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The Croatian police arrested me and drove me in an APC to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you told why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, to my surprise, on that occasion the police commander, Mr. Nikola Jukanec, with whom I negotiated during Flash, and that's when I met him. It went on for four days. During the arrest he said: I'm sorry, but these are my orders from Zagreb to put handcuffs on you and to arrest you. That's what he did. And he took me to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why he said he was sorry?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I think that he did not agree with this kind of task because he was aware of my role throughout, and he knew that during our negotiations, during Flash, we saved many lives, people were not killed. Had such an arrangement not been made, then many more people would have lost their lives, and I don't think that any normal person would be willing to accept that kind of reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long were you held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: And then I was driven back to Pakrac, to the police station, where my friends were waiting for me, Obrad Ivanovic and Miroslav Grozdanic, and there were a few ministers from the government of the Republic of Serb Krajina and We squabbled about how all of this had been done. We protested quite a bit, especially I, because many men were arrested and taken to prison, and for some we didn't know where they were detained. And then sometime in the evening, about 10.00 in the evening, the three of us were taken away by a police patrol at the command of the commander Josko Moric and they took us up to an elevation there and they left us alone. And then three -- from three directions vehicles were moving. We didn't know what was going on. The first one that reached us was a UN APC, and the soldiers were throwing themselves at us to protect us. We didn't know what was going on, but later on we realised that from the other two directions there were Croats. We didn't know whether it was the special police or the army, they were asking for us to be handed over. They were screaming, yelling, for all three of us, especially me, and they were asking for us to be handed over. However, Jusuf Aralfi, head of the UN sector who had brought these soldiers took us back to the police station and told me: The three of you have to spend the night at the police station tonight, otherwise these people are going to liquidate you because they don't want to see you in this setting again. They provided us with security for a few days, both the UN troops, and also they ordered the Croatian police to be there, to be nearby, so that their extremists would not come and do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Then we stayed in Pakrac. We continued negotiating on the normalisation of relations. That evening we went to my friend's home. There were guards there. We had contacts with our own countrymen and also with international representatives, so that people who wanted to stay could have some kind of security, safety of movement, freedom of movement, and they could get their documents. On the other hand, those who wanted to leave should be allowed to leave, convoys should be organised, and all of this was done by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back in time, back to 1990. In the summer of 1990, did something happen in Srb?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a big gathering of Serbs from a large part of the Republic of Croatia. Some people estimate that there were even 250.000 to 300.000 people there. I was there, too. It was a very impressive gathering. Jovo Raskovic, Milan Babic, Dusan Zelembaba and others spoke, and cultural autonomy of the Serbs was proclaimed then. The Serb National Council was elected then, Dr. Milan Babic at the proposal of Jovo Raskovic. There wasn't a proper vote there. It was done by acclamation. A lot of people accepted that Milan Babic should be president of the Serb council. Jovan Raskovic was president of the party and he didn't like to hold too many positions, so he wanted to share office with other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there later a conflict between Milan Babic and Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, they went their separate ways and there was a conflict, too. Jovan Raskovic was being called too soft, not tough enough, and Milan Babic, of course, was no competition for Jovan Raskovic, but then he split the SDS into the SDS Krajina, too. And the rest of the SDS, which was a majority, a vast majority, was the SDS of the Republic of Croatia. So Milan Babic succeeded and created the SDS SAO Krajina. Although, from that area when he proclaimed the SDS SAO Krajina, there were many members. I think even more the people from there stayed with Jovan Raskovic, the SDS of Jovan Raskovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did that split occur between Milan Babic and Jovan Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, I can say that it was right after what happened in Srb, because obviously Milan Babic started feeling very important and powerful and then Jovan Raskovic bothered him because he needed the position of the president of the council. Jovan Raskovic did not have time for personal conflicts like this. He wanted to organise the party properly, he wanted to have as many reasonable, normal people around him as much as possible, so he didn't really want to waste time on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you first heard about Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, as for the name of Milan Martic, I first heard of it sometime in August 1990 when the first barricades were placed in the area of Knin. Very soon it was heard in the public that a police inspector, a police commander, I don't know exactly what position he held at the time, had ordered that or organised the placing of these barricades, these roadblocks. And in that area through the media, he was felt to be a new hero of the Serbs who had the strength and power to oppose, first of all, the institutions of the Republic of Croatia that could no longer function in that area where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he, himself, appear in the media?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, it was on television, too. I remember his statement that this police that he headed no longer obeyed the Zagreb police, that this was the people's police, that they had nothing to do with them, and he, Milan Martic, confirmed that. He was quite clear on that, quite unequivocal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When he was talking about the people's police that no longer obeyed Zagreb, do you know what area he was talking about, referring to? The police in what area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, I think that at that time it was these five or six municipalities, Benkovac, Knin, Lapac, Gracac, Korenica. That was the beginning, and later on it spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was the -- what was the purpose or what did the barricades do? What did you know about the barricades?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, the point was to place roadblocks so that Croat forces could not enter, Croat forces that would want to restore control, and also all those who were considered unwelcome, who had intentions that were unwelcome at the time with some other ideas. I don't know what else. But primarily it was against the police of the Republic of Croatia, so that they would not come, replace different people, and restore their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what area did the barricades blockade?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, I think that at that time it was the municipality of Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, Lapac, Korenica, I don't know whether it was Obrovac, too; I cannot remember. That was the beginning. Later on it spread to Banija and Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken about the media, both in terms of how the media portrayed Milan Martic and also about Milan Martic appearing himself in the media. What media are you talking about? Where is this media from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, the media were from Belgrade and Zagreb. If they were from Zagreb, then they presented as terrorists. The Serbs were then also called the Chetnik gangs. And when Belgrade reported on it, they said: The Serb heroes who dared, who were courageous. So it depended on the media, how they portrayed it. The Belgrade spoke of it in a favourable sense, the Zagreb media in an unfavourable sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, I'm going to show you a clip, and for this we're going to need to switch to the Sanction. And it's a clip it's V000-3862. Rather, it's a clip from that video exhibit, and I'm going to -- before the clip is shown, I'm going to distribute a translation of the clip, which will also appear on the screen in synchronised fashion to the speaking. This is a clip that was used in the opening statement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said we are going to switch over to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are going to switch over to Sanction which is -- and this is for the audio-visual booth. They switch the video evidence to Sanction. So if you put on video evidence -- sorry, I'm told it's computer evidence. This is new to us, too, this -- having these different elements. So it's computer evidence. If we switch to computer evidence, this tape will be played and hopefully it will be coordinated and it will work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, were you able to watch and understand that entire clip or do I need to play it again?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you recognise who was speaking in the beginning of the clip?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I recognised the voice, and later on I recognised the face of Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was this clip similar to media broadcasts of Mr. Martic that you described earlier for the Court that were occurring at this time in August 1990/September 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move this clip into evidence, please. And I suppose what I would do is move into evidence the transcript and the clip which is being handed to the usher and to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What is that called, DVD or CD-ROM? What is that called? We cannot admit "clip," I want to admit that piece of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know if it's a DVD or a CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: CD is an audio, DVD would also show pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, then it's a DVD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told it's just called a video clip. Okay. The video clip is then admitted into evidence. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Along - I'm sorry - with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Together with the transcript. It being an object where my experience is that then it would be Exhibit A and not 4. Is that not how you do things here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. Ordinarily it would just be given the next exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's no distinction between objects and documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then the disk with the clip will be admitted into evidence as Exhibit number 4; and the translation, the English translation, will be admitted into evidence as Exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've identified in your testimony a number of Serb leaders in Croatia who took a different position from you, from your positions, during 1990. After August of 1990 and into 1991, did these leaders talk about being threatened by Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did talk about that. They used every rally where something bad would be said about the Serbs, and bad things were said, that they were over-represented in the police or as managers, that the Serbs should not be a political factor. And also they took advantage of the iconography at these rallies. And all of this made them think of the independent state of Croatia from the Second World War, and they were saying that what lay in store for the Serbs yet again was what happened in 1941, 1942, and 1943. That is why they avoided all contacts and stopped all contacts with the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were some of the leaders that spoke this way during 1990 and into 1991?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost it was Milan Babic, Djoko Vjestica, Stipovac, Marko Dobrijevic. And then there was Dali Djurastovic [phoen] from Lapac, Bosko Bozanic from Korenica. They figured most prominently as far as such speech was concerned. It's not Stipovac, it's Stikovac. I see what was typed out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Did -- in your view, were these threats from Croatia that were being described by these Serb leaders accurate or were they being exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, it was exaggerated, because there weren't any concrete threats that there would be killings or massacres. The iconography that was present at rallies was resorted to. If there would be 300 to 500 people, there would be among them people with Ustasha iconography. This is how people were intimidated because this was shown on television and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say it was shown on television, which television are you talking about? You've already described how there were two sides to the television. Which one are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Now we're talking about the Serbian television, Belgrade television, that portrayed HDZ rallies and other gatherings in Croatia. And when a few people like that would appear, or several such persons, I don't know how many, would appear with that kind of iconography, they would focus on that. So one would get the impression that this was predominant at such a gathering. And then they would also use statements made by Tudjman, that he was proud of the fact that his wife was not a Serb or a Jew, and that was rather offensive. And they interpreted that sentence of his as a bad message being sent out to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what effect -- were you able to tell if these statements that were being made by politicians about the threats and that were being made by the Serbian media, were you able to tell if that had any effect on the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, it caused quite a bit of anxiety and fear among the Serb population because people additionally felt that the former independent state of Croatia was coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is probably a convenient time. It's almost an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. By the time we come back -- I'm told we've got to take a break of at least 30 minutes. By the time we come -- quarter past 6.00, okay. Court adjourned. We will come back at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again you're reminded that you're still bound by the declaration, Mr. Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, in 1990 did you attend a meeting in Belgrade with Jovic and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was in 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I think it was in November or December, towards the end of the year. There was a rally of Serbs from Croatia. They went to meet with Jovic and Milosevic. It was a meeting, rather, not a rally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who -- who went to that meeting from the -- which Serbs from Croatia went to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Serbs from Knin, Gracac, Benkovac, Lika, a few from Banija, and some from Western Slavonia -- or rather, only Veljko Vukic and I were from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How many Serbs went to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: There were some 30 or so of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was -- why were these people allowed to go to this meeting and why were they selected to go to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I don't know who called the meeting or selected the people, but I was informed by Veljko Vukic, who was a member of the regional SDS board of Western Slavonia -- or rather, of Slavonia at the time about this meeting. And when he told me about it, I decided to go there to see what it was about. And I was told that it would be a good idea to present our experiences and the problems facing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the meeting about? What was the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: When I arrived, I saw that the aim of those who spoke at the meeting was to present their views on what was happening in Croatia. A man called Mlinar from Benkovac spoke, as he did at every such meeting. He had been in an incident in Benkovac. And then Djoko Vjestica from Gracac spoke. Some other people who I didn't know. They spoke in very strong terms, speaking about women crying and children being afraid. I saw that what they were saying did not quite correspond to the truth, at least not in the area they were from. These areas were inhabited by Serbs, and the situation they were in was not the way they described it. At one point I managed to take the floor, and this was difficult because everybody wanted to speak, and I said I did not quite agree with what they had said because if it was difficult to be a Serb in Knin, Srb, or Gracac, what must it like to be a Serb in Zagreb, or Kutina, or Novska, where there were fewer Serbs or where they are in the minority. I said if that were so they would need an armoured vehicle to go to work. And I said there was no need to be so euphoric, to exaggerate in this way. When I was criticised for saying this, I said I only wanted to present the situation as it was and not to make a big fuss about it. However, I was not successful in my attempts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that some of these people, Djoko Vjestica and others, spoke about women crying and children being afraid. Could you elaborate just a little bit more about what kinds of things they talked about and what did they say they were afraid of.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: For example, Mlinar came there. This had to do with a well-known incident. He had a scar on his neck. And the media and he, himself, said that Croatian extremists had attempted to cut his throat. I think that later it was proved that he, himself, fabricated this in order to draw attention to himself. I'm not saying that there weren't any incidents of that sort, but they were probably just threats, not attempts to cut someone's throat. They said they were afraid of being killed, of being expelled, that they were seeking protection, that they couldn't stay there like that. That was the gist of what they were trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And these were Serbs who were afraid?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were Serbs who were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And to be clear, they were afraid of whom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: They were afraid of the new Croatian politics, the Croatian police, and the Croatian army, and of course I responded. Because I couldn't accept that people in Srb, Knin, Gracac, Lapac, Korenica, where they were in the majority, 80 or 90 per cent, would feel more threatened than Serbs in Zagreb, Knin or Karlovac who certainly had to be facing bigger problems than they -- than they were. So I thought that this was something these individuals were saying. I would have understood it if these Serbs had been from an area where the HDZ was in power, but what these people were saying was something that they saw perhaps as a way of gaining some advantage for themselves. I thought that if people were afraid, then we should try to talk to people, not just raise tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, was Milan Babic at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He liked to be on his own and to be someone important. He wouldn't have attended a meeting like that, but his associates were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there -- after the meeting with Jovic, was there also a meeting with Milosevic or was that the same meeting?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: What I said is something I said when we met with Milosevic -- actually, I was speaking of both meetings. When we came to see Milosevic, that was when I spoke and took the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in 1990, after August of 1990, and into 1991, what was the relationship between Milan Babic and Milan Martic, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: From what I heard, they got on well. They were not against one another. I think they didn't interfere with each other's work. Babic was politically active and Martic had his own activities. However, I never saw the two of them together. I would meet with Babic but not with Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before 1990, before the events in 1990, how -- can you explain how -- to your knowledge, how the police was organised.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: It had its active-duty composition, its reserve composition. It was organised by municipality. There were no counties then, but communities of interest or something like that. They had a secretariat, not a ministry, at republican level, and then lower down at municipal level. So there were the active-duty police and the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after -- or let's say around August 1990 and thereafter, do you know how Milan Martic started to organise the police in the areas where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Whiting, the witness hasn't told us about any organisation by Mr. Martic. You are now suggesting to him that Mr. Martic organised something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was following on the answer earlier about the people's police in the municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, Lapac. But I can phrase the question differently, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do, because you hadn't linked it to that previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, you told us earlier about the people's police and the statements of Milan Martic after August of 1990. Do you recall testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I asked you which municipalities he -- Milan Martic was referring to when he was referring to the people's police.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I think he was referring to these four or five municipalities such as Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, Lapac, and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know what was happening with respect to the police in those municipalities at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that they had some form of mobilisation and that barricades had been set up. I heard that some people left the police force, and then of course others were recruited to bring it up to manpower levels. However, I was not familiar with the details because I had no access to what was happening; I just heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you hear about what left and who joined the police in those areas, in those municipalities we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Later on I heard from Mirko Raskovic that he was among those who left the police force. He said that he had parted ways with Martic, but I also heard that Croats left the police force and that Serbs were recruited to bring it up to manpower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know if Milan Martic had any role in what was happening with those police forces in those municipalities at that time, after August 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: From what I heard and not from direct knowledge, I heard that he had absolute authority in the police when it came to appointing policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, Mr. Whiting. The witness has been telling us about what he heard and not what he observed -- he's not taking from direct information and direct knowledge, rather. And now he's talking specifically about the accused. And once again, he says clearly -- I'm sorry: "From what I heard and not from direct knowledge, I heard that he had absolute authority in the police." Are you going to call this person he heard from and who that person is, and can you tell us who that person is he heard from?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was going to follow up, Your Honour, to find out from what sources he heard this from. And of course there will be other witnesses who will testify about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you will, please, because for almost a page he's been talking about what I heard and what I didn't hear, and nothing from direct knowledge, which makes this testimony very difficult to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, no doubt you heard the intervention of the Chamber, and with respect to what you've been testifying about what you heard about Milan Martic in 1991, could you tell us where you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: One heard on the media that people were leaving, that others were recruited, that the reserve force was being mobilised. The media spoke about this. I also heard it from some individuals when I was in Belgrade, who spoke to me about the police of the SAO Krajina being formed and who were from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you -- what can you tell us about these individuals that you spoke to in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: These were people who disagreed with the policy of Milan Babic and Milan Martic. For example, Zdravko Zecevic, who was a dissident at the time, but who then embraced that option and became the prime minister. Sergej Veselinovic was another such person who was with him, and later on they changed their standpoints a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These two people who you've just identified, Zecevic and Zelenovic [sic], what was their relationship to the Krajina? That is, were they -- did they have a relationship with the Krajina? What was the source of their information?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Zecevic from Benkovac and Sergej Veselinovic from Obrovac. They were in the SDS together with Jovan Raskovic, and they were not in the SAO SDS of Milan Babic. This belonged to the SAO of Krajina as territory, but their viewpoints were closer to those of the SDS of Jovan Raskovic rather than the SDS of Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But did the views of those two individuals later change?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. Later they changed. This began sometime in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified specifically that you heard that he, Milan Martic, had absolute authority in the police when it came to appointing policemen. Do you remember where you heard that from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: If you're referring to the year 1991, the two men I mentioned; if you mean later on, I saw it when we had the government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell us about that, what you saw later on.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Later on, at government sessions when we spoke of staffing and appointing people in the police, from the assistant minister to chiefs of the police in the municipalities, nothing could be done without the proposal and agreement of Martic. Krsta Zarkovic was appointed assistant minister for Western Slavonia at his initiative. He was the main person in charge of staffing in the ministry of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that you saw this in the government sessions, what period of time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This was in 1992 to February 1993. From February 1992 to February 1993, that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you ever witness Milan Martic talking to subordinates?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion I attended a government session, and I don't know who it was who came, but you could see that he was a person who had authority, who was obeyed, whose orders were complied with. And if someone failed to comply with an order of his, he could be quite rough. He could be angry. He could threaten that they would be replaced, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that that you saw that at the government session, that one occasion that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: This was in the course of 1992. I know that there were problems with the police in Eastern Slavonia. I don't know what the name was that was discussed, but in the lower part of Lika and Dalmatia because some people probably wanted to appoint their own man as chief of police, and he would not allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Going back again to 1991, was there anything in the media about -- that talked about Martic's role in the police in the municipalities that we were talking about, in the area that we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Both in the Croatian and the Serbian media, his name was often mentioned, the name of Milan Martic. Martic's police here and Martic's police there. It was mentioned very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was there anything -- do you recall -- are you able to recall today anything specifically mentioned about what his role was in that police?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: You mean 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I think military war operations in the area of Dalmatia were mentioned, that it was mentioned that the police of SAO Krajina and the army had committed a crime in Skabrnja. It was also said that this had also happened in Kostajnica and other places in Banija and in Dalmatia. I don't recall all the villages right now, but I know that this was shown on the Croatian media as actions of the police of the SAO Krajina and the army, the JNA, which was called the Serbo-Chetnik army, the Jugo-Communist army, and other names like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you some more questions in a moment about what you heard about crimes in 1991, but I want to go back to my question because I don't think you've answered my question yet, which is: Did you hear in the media in 1991 about -- that described in some way what Martic's role was in the municipalities around Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Only that he organised the police of the SAO Krajina, that he formed and organised it. When I say "he," I'm referring to Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was that in the Serbian media, the Croatian media, or both?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In both. The Croatian media spoke of it in unfavourable terms, and the Serbian media represented it as a brave action by a responsible person, who was a hero. Very favourable things were written about him because he was standing up to the Croatian police. The Croatian media showed it in an unfavourable light. They were renegades, rebels, and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Babic -- do you know if Milan Babic ever had control over the police in the -- in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: From what I heard, no; and knowing Milan Martic as I knew him, I think Babic was unable to have any kind of control over that. Babic dealt with politics and Martic with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And since this is important, if you could just elaborate on what you're saying. "Knowing Milan Martic as I knew him." What did you know about him that leads you to say what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: As far as I was able to get to know him at the government sessions, Mr. Martic never allowed anyone to interfere in his job. He felt that he was able and competent to organise and order his own ministry in the way he knew. He chose his own associates and formed the police like that. He would not allow any politician to interfere or to make suggestions to him. Later on I saw that in Western Slavonia he replaced people. He brought a man called Veselinovic from Knin there. And this only went to show that he had absolute authority. He didn't ask anyone in Western Slavonia who should be appointed, but he brought a man called Veselinovic from the other area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say that you got to know him at the government sessions, that's which government, in which time period?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: At the government sessions of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from February 1992 to February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- and the incident that you just told us about when he brought a man called Veselinovic into Western Slavonia, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: That happened later. That was in 1995, I think. Vaso Ostolucanin was replaced who was in the police there, and Veselinovic was brought in. I heard that personally from Vaso Ostolucanin because we were friends and we knew each other well. He was close to our policy and our views, and he probably did not suit the then-policy of the Republic of Serb Krajina, so he was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Several times when you've referred to your seeing things at the government sessions you talk about this year period from February 1992 to February 1993. Again, was there something happened around February 1993 that changed your participation in the government sessions? You've testified about this already, but I just want to make it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: In 1993, in February, that was just before I was replaced, the Daruvar Agreement had been concluded, I can't remember anything else right this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But did you stop attending the government sessions at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: I stopped attending after February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. What were you able to -- what was -- in your observation, what was Milan Martic's reputation? You've told us a little bit about him, but could you talk about his reputation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: He was a highly appreciated person on the government and also among the Serbs in that area. After the corridor was made in Posavina, his reputation skyrocketed. He was promoted on account of that. He was celebrated in Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. And after that, I think he had absolute authority in government, especially gained during the course of 1992. And everybody listened to what he had to say, from the prime minister to the president of the republic, let alone ministers and assistant ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1991 and 1992, and you can -- I invite you to specify more exactly in your answer, what did you observe about Milan Martic's attitude about Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: His view was very set. He did not consider Croatia his country any longer. It was a Serb Krajina, and he was not in favour of any kind of talks with such a state and such a policy, that we were supposed to work for recognition and joining the association of Serb lands, Republika Srpska, and Serbia. Those were his own landmarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did you observe him to espouse those views?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, from when I met him, and I met him in February 1992, from then onwards, that's what was being said at government sessions. And usually the first item would be the political and security situation, and that's when I realised what the views concerning Croatia were and generally what kind of behaviour should be espoused in various activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Martic saw a place for Croats living in the Serb areas in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, I think he did not have any understanding for that because when we had a government session concerning the return of refugees, our views differed and we talked about the process of demilitarisation and the Vance plan. Martic was against demilitarisation, which was a pre-condition for the return of refugees, and he was also -- or rather, he had no understanding for the return of refugees, and that was the opinion of most of the members of government, and that is why we had a government session in 1992, the end of 1992. It was in Western Slavonia, and it was devoted to that particular subject to see how to make it possible for the Croats to return. The Croats were leaving the area from Benkovac, Obrovac. I think that there were some Croats remaining only in Knin. And during 1992 -- well, the war was in 1991 and some were killed and some left, and during 1992 they were leaving Krajina and going to Croatia. That's when the exchanges took place, too, through the UN checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you some more precise questions about this topic. First of all, you've made a reference to the Vance plan. What is the Vance plan?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Well, the Vance plan was an agreement that was signed on the 2nd of January, 1992. It implied a cease-fire and deployment of UN forces in the war-afflicted areas. We adopted it during the month of March and April 1992 at the Assembly of RSK, and it was accepted there. And it was supposed to be carried out. One of the very important points was the demilitarisation of the area, which meant that long rifles and heavy weaponry should be put in warehouses with two keys. The keys would be held by the UN and the police and army of the RSK, and that only short-barrelled guns could be carried, that is to say, only the police could have their guns, wear them on their belts, and that is a major -- that is what led to a major clash. Mr. Martic was the mainstay of this, and he was supported by the president of the republic, that is to say, not to respect demilitarisation. So people still carried large weapons in SAO Krajina and in large part of the Republic of Serb Krajina. Only we in Western Slavonia carried out demilitarisation during the course of 1992. And on the 2nd of September, 1992, Marrack Goulding, under-secretary of the UN, came to Okucani to congratulate us and to pay tribute to us. And other parts of the SAO Krajina, that is to say, Eastern Slavonia and SAO Krajina namely, I'm sorry, never carried out demilitarisation because Mr. Martic and people who worked with him in the Ministry of Defence thought that it was only with weapons that Krajina could be safeguarded and defended and that demilitarisation could not be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Dzakula, let me ask you a few follow-up questions about the subject of demilitarisation. First of all, under the Vance plan, what area was going to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The entire area that was afflicted by war from behind Zadar, what I drew on the map for you, and it was to be like an inkblot. And that is where UN forces were to be deployed, in Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, and this part of Krajina, which was part of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as part of this demilitarisation, was something going to happen with the army, the Yugoslav army, that was known then as the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The JNA, or rather, the army of the RSK had to be fully disarmed. Heavy weaponry, cannons, tanks, Howitzers, I'm not very knowledgeable about this, had to be in these warehouses as agreed, and how far away they had to be from the line of conflict. The army had to wear civilian clothing, and only the police could be in uniform, and they could only have short-barrelled weapons. That was only carried out in Western Slavonia, where the army was wearing civilian clothes and where they had disarmed, whereas the heavy weapons were locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did the Vance plan also have any provisions relating to refugees?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The next point was the refugee -- the return of refugees. Since we carried out the demilitarisation of Western Slavonia, we were bringing pressure to bear in order to have the refugee returns start. And we agreed that in Pakrac and an area near Pakrac the flow of -- the Croats who fled should return, and there was another part of Pakrac that was under Croat military control, and Serbs were supposed to be returned there. That was our plan. However, it was not carried out and this was never achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now you referred to this special session of the government that was held at the end of 1992. Where was that session held?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: The session was held in Vrbovljani, a village near Okucani. The agenda was the return of refugees, due to this pressure that we from Western Slavonia made, and that's why this government session was held there. The prime minister, most members of the government, came to Okucani first. That's where they had talks. And the information I received was that they had already agreed that our proposal should not be adopted, that is to say, that refugees should not be returned. There was a very heated debate at the government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm just going to interrupt you for a moment there, Mr. Dzakula. How did you receive that information that the proposal should not be adopted, that had already been agreed?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO DZAKULA
utterances.text: That's what Stevo Bogic from Eastern Slavonia, the deputy prime minister told me. We were close. And he was sorry that I did not receive support, and he said to me: You will remain on your own. You will not have support for the return of your Serbs in Western Slavonia. As far as I can, I will help you, but you will not receive support. That was in Okucani, and that's the information that he brought he five minutes before the government session actually started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more questions about what happened at the government session, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are at the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are at the hour. Okay. The matter will then stand adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of January, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
